title: THEY CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. BUT THE BIBLE NEVER DID.
paragraphs: THEY CALLED HER A PROSTITUTE. BUT THE BIBLE NEVER DID.
Mary Magdalene, the scandal history attached to her name, and the breathtaking truth about the woman Jesus called by name.
What if one of the most famous stories you have heard about a woman in the Bible was never actually written in the Bible?
What if generations of Christians repeated a description of her that Matthew never recorded, Mark never confirmed, Luke never claimed, and John never even suggested?
And what if the truth about this woman is far more powerful than the scandal people attached to her name?
Her name was Mary Magdalene.
For centuries, her name has been associated with prostitution, sexual immorality, and the familiar image of a fallen woman rescued by Jesus Christ.
Paintings portrayed her that way. Sermons repeated the story. Films reinforced it. Eventually, for many believers, the association became so familiar that it felt like Scripture itself.
But there is a problem.
The four Gospels never identify Mary Magdalene as a prostitute. Not once.
And when you discover where that reputation came from, something remarkable happens.
You begin to see how easily a human tradition can become confused with biblical truth.
You begin to recognize the danger of telling someone's story without first listening to what God actually revealed.
And most importantly, you begin to see a woman whose real testimony does not need an invented scandal to demonstrate the extraordinary grace of Jesus Christ.
Because Mary Magdalene's story was never meant to make us fascinated with her supposed sexual past.
It was meant to direct our attention toward her risen Savior.
And the moment Jesus spoke her name outside an empty tomb, everything changed.
But before we reach that garden, we need to return to the Scriptures.
Because the truth begins with something Luke actually wrote.

In Luke 8:1–3, Jesus was traveling through cities and villages, proclaiming the good news of the kingdom of God. The Twelve were with Him, along with several women who had experienced healing and deliverance.
Among them was Mary Magdalene.
Luke 8:2 describes her in the original Greek:
Μαρία ἡ καλουμένη Μαγδαληνή, ἀφ’ ἧς δαιμόνια ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει.
A faithful translation is:
"Mary, who was called Magdalene, from whom seven demons had gone out."
Read that again.
Not seven husbands.
Not seven lovers.
Not seven sexual sins.
Seven demons.
That is what the text says.
And that distinction matters.
The Greek word δαιμόνια (daimonia) means demons. The expression ἑπτὰ ἐξεληλύθει communicates that seven demons had gone out from her.
Luke identifies Mary as a woman who had experienced extraordinary spiritual deliverance.
He does not identify her former occupation.
He does not describe her sexual history.
He does not connect her demonization with prostitution.
And Scripture gives us no authority to invent those details.

We must also be careful not to turn the number seven into a secret biography. Although seven can carry symbolic significance elsewhere in Scripture, Luke gives no explanation that would allow us to identify seven particular sins or seven stages of Mary's past.
The text tells us that she was delivered.
That is already a remarkable testimony.
Imagine living under a bondage so severe that your name becomes associated with seven demons.
We do not know exactly what Mary endured. The Gospels do not describe her symptoms, the duration of her suffering, or the circumstances of her deliverance.
But we do know this.
Jesus had set her free.
And afterward, Mary was among those who followed Him.
That is where the story becomes deeply personal.
Because some people reading this know what it means to have a painful chapter of life become the only chapter other people remember.
Maybe they know your addiction but not your recovery.
Your divorce but not your repentance.
Your failure but not your restoration.
Your breakdown but not the quiet courage it took to get out of bed the following morning.
Maybe people still introduce you through the worst thing that ever happened to you.
And perhaps the hardest part is that you have started introducing yourself that way too.
But consider what Luke does with Mary's story.
He tells us about her deliverance, then shows us her discipleship.
The woman who had been oppressed was now following Jesus.
And she was not merely standing at a distance.
Luke 8:3 explains that these women were helping provide for Jesus and His followers from their own resources.
Mary Magdalene was part of that group.
Think about the significance.
The Gospel does not present her as an unnamed background character whose only importance was her suffering.
She was a named follower of Christ, associated with a group of women who materially supported His ministry.
The Greek expression διηκόνουν αὐτοῖς (diēkonoun autois) describes their service or provision for them.
This was practical discipleship.
Their faith had hands.
Their gratitude became service.
And there is a beautiful lesson here for every believer who has ever wondered whether ordinary resources can serve an eternal purpose.
Not everyone preaches before a crowd.
Not everyone travels to distant nations.
Not everyone writes books, teaches Scripture, or leads a ministry.
But people who faithfully give, serve, encourage, pray, and provide can participate meaningfully in the work of spreading the Gospel.
Mary Magdalene's example reminds us that supporting Christ's mission is not insignificant simply because it happens away from the spotlight.
Yet we must not confuse her faithful support with an obligation imposed upon every believer to fund a particular ministry.
Christian generosity is meant to be sincere and willing.
As 2 Corinthians 9:7 teaches, giving should not be driven by reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That distinction matters.
Grace is not a product we purchase.
God's favor cannot be bought.
Mary's story gives us an example of that kind of grateful service.
Now comes the question that has confused Christians for generations.
If the Gospels never call Mary Magdalene a prostitute, where did the idea originate?
To understand that, we need to examine another woman in Luke's Gospel.
In Luke 7:36–50, an unnamed woman enters the house of Simon the Pharisee while Jesus is dining there.
She is described as a sinner.
She weeps at Jesus' feet, wets them with her tears, wipes them with her hair, kisses them, and anoints them with perfume.
It is one of the most moving scenes in the Gospel.
A woman enters a room where she is already judged.
A religious host silently questions why Jesus would allow her to touch Him.
And Jesus responds by exposing the difference between self-righteousness and grateful love.
He tells a parable about two debtors.
One owes much.
The other owes less.
Both debts are forgiven.
Then Jesus asks which debtor will love the creditor more.
The answer is obvious.
The one who was forgiven more.
Jesus then points toward the woman's extraordinary expression of love.
And in Luke 7:48, He tells her:
"Thy sins are forgiven." (KJV)
It is a breathtaking moment.
But notice something crucial.
Luke never names this woman Mary Magdalene.
He does not identify her as a prostitute either.
The description of her as a sinner does not specify the nature of her sins.
The connection between this unnamed woman and Mary Magdalene is not made by Luke.
It was made through later interpretation.
And the placement of these stories helped that interpretation spread.
The unnamed woman appears near the end of Luke chapter 7.
Mary Magdalene is introduced at the beginning of Luke chapter 8.
Two women.
Two passages.
One Gospel.
But no statement that they are the same person.
Then another Mary entered the conversation.
Mary of Bethany, the sister of Martha and Lazarus.
In John 12:1–8, Mary of Bethany anoints Jesus' feet with expensive perfume and wipes them with her hair.
That account shares certain details with the unnamed woman's actions in Luke 7, although the settings and surrounding narratives differ.
Over time, some Christian interpreters connected the unnamed sinful woman, Mary of Bethany, and Mary Magdalene into one composite figure.
One especially influential moment occurred in AD 591.
Pope Gregory I, often called Gregory the Great, preached a homily in which he associated the unnamed sinful woman in Luke 7 with Mary Magdalene and connected the seven demons with a fullness of vice.
His interpretation became highly influential in Western Christianity.
But here is an important historical distinction.
Gregory did not invent every association from nothing, and his homily did not explicitly establish that Mary Magdalene had worked as a prostitute.

Earlier interpretive traditions had already explored connections between these women. Gregory helped consolidate and popularize an identification that later Western preaching, art, and devotion would develop further.
The specific prostitute image became part of that broader tradition.
Meanwhile, Eastern Christian traditions generally maintained clearer distinctions between Mary Magdalene, Mary of Bethany, and the unnamed sinful woman.
This history is important because it helps explain how a familiar religious picture can become more detailed than the biblical text that supposedly supports it.
A sermon becomes a tradition.
A tradition shapes a painting.
A painting shapes a film.
A film shapes a generation's imagination.
And eventually someone hears the name Mary Magdalene and thinks immediately of prostitution.
Not because Luke said it.
Not because John confirmed it.
But because centuries of storytelling made the association feel unquestionable.
This is not a reason to despise Christian history or dismiss every ancient teacher.
It is a reason to test interpretations against Scripture.
The Bereans were commended in Acts 17:11 because they examined the Scriptures to see whether what they heard was true.
We should do the same.
Even when a claim is familiar.
Even when it comes from a respected preacher.
Even when we have believed it since childhood.
The question must remain:
What does the Word of God actually say?
And this is where Mary's story begins to confront something deeper than a historical misunderstanding.
How many times have we confidently repeated something about another person without knowing whether it was true?
How many reputations have been damaged by stories that grew more dramatic each time they were told?
How many people have spent years trying to escape a label they never deserved?
And how often have Christians defended a tradition more passionately than they have examined the text?
Mary Magdalene cannot answer our questions.
But the Scriptures can correct our assumptions.
And perhaps that correction is something some of us need more than we want to admit.
Because the Gospel does not give us permission to exaggerate another person's shame just to make God's grace appear greater.
God's grace is already greater than we can measure.
We do not need to invent sin to magnify the Savior.
We do not need to create a scandal to make redemption beautiful.
The cross of Jesus Christ is sufficient.
Now consider what happens later in Mary's story.
The crowds that once followed Jesus begin to disappear.
The hostility intensifies.
Jesus is arrested.
He is condemned.
And He is crucified.
The One who had delivered Mary is now hanging upon a Roman cross.
The One who had spoken with divine authority is being mocked.
The One who had healed the broken is bleeding before a watching world.
And Mary Magdalene is named among the women present at the crucifixion.
John 19:25 places her near the cross of Jesus, alongside His mother and other women.
Matthew 27:55–56 and Mark 15:40–41 also identify her among the women who witnessed the crucifixion, describing their presence from a distance.
The accounts emphasize different vantage points, but together they establish something unmistakable.
Mary Magdalene witnessed the suffering and death of Jesus.
Pause there.
She had followed the One who set her free.
And now she was watching Him die.
Imagine the confusion.
The grief.
The terrible silence that follows when the person you trusted seems to have been taken from you.
We must not pretend to know every thought in Mary's heart.
Scripture does not record them.
But the events themselves were devastating.
Jesus was crucified.
His body was buried.
The tomb was sealed.
And the disciples faced a darkness they had not expected.
There are seasons in our own lives when we know something of that bewilderment.
We prayed, but the diagnosis remained.
We trusted, but the relationship collapsed.
We obeyed, but the door closed.
We believed God was working, yet all we could see was a grave.
Sometimes the most painful question is not whether God exists.
It is why the God we love seems silent when everything is falling apart.
Mary's story does not answer every question about suffering.
But it leads us to a garden where death does not have the final word.
John chapter 20 opens early on the first day of the week.
It is still dark.
Mary Magdalene comes to the tomb.
And the stone has been taken away.
She runs to Simon Peter and the disciple whom Jesus loved.
Her conclusion is not that Jesus has risen.
She believes someone has taken His body.
The disciples come to the tomb.
They see evidence that something extraordinary has happened.
Then they return.
But Mary remains outside, weeping.
This is one of the most tender moments in all four Gospels.
The woman once delivered from seven demons is standing outside an empty tomb.
And she is crying.
She looks inside and sees two angels.
They ask why she is weeping.
She explains that her Lord has been taken away and she does not know where He has been laid.
Then she turns and sees someone standing nearby.
It is Jesus.
But she does not recognize Him.
He asks why she is weeping and whom she is seeking.
She supposes He is the gardener.
And then, in John 20:16, everything changes.
Jesus says one word.
Μαριάμ — Mariam.
"Mary."
The Greek text preserves a form of her name that reflects its Semitic background.
And the next moment is unforgettable.
She turns toward Him and responds:
Ῥαββουνί — Rabbouni.
John explains the meaning as "Teacher."
The expression is a Semitic form of address preserved in the Greek Gospel.
We do not need to invent the exact language Jesus spoke in that moment or claim knowledge of His tone.
John gives us something more than enough.
Jesus called her by name.
And she recognized Him.
One moment she believed her Lord was gone.
The next, she was standing before the risen Christ.
The tomb was empty not because death had stolen Him, but because death could not hold Him.
The cross had not defeated Jesus.
His sacrifice had accomplished the work of redemption.
And His resurrection confirmed the victory.
This is the heart of Christianity.
Not merely that Jesus was a compassionate teacher.
Not merely that He welcomed people whom society rejected.
Not merely that He restored broken lives.
But that the sinless Son of God died for our sins, was buried, and rose again, according to the Scriptures.
As Paul declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4, Christ died for our sins, was buried, and rose again on the third day.
Without that truth, Mary's experience would be only a story about grief.
With it, her testimony becomes an announcement of hope for the world.
And there is something astonishing about the role Jesus gives her.
In John 20:17, He instructs Mary to go to His brothers and deliver His message.
She obeys.
John 20:18 records her announcement:
Ἑώρακα τὸν κύριον — Heōraka ton kyrion.
"I have seen the Lord."
Not, "I have finally escaped my reputation."
Not, "People now understand my past."
Not, "My name has been cleared."
"I have seen the Lord."
That is her testimony.
That is the center of her story.
The risen Jesus Christ.
Mary Magdalene is among the earliest recorded witnesses of the resurrection, and John's Gospel gives her a remarkable role in announcing the risen Lord to the disciples.
In later Christian tradition, she would sometimes be honored with the title "apostle to the apostles," reflecting this mission of announcing the resurrection.
That title is a later description, not a direct quotation from the Gospel text.
But the event it celebrates is biblical.
Jesus entrusted Mary with a message.
And she delivered it.
Think about the contrast.
For centuries, popular imagination would focus on a sexual history the Gospels never assigned to her.
But John focuses on the testimony Jesus actually gave her.
She had seen the risen Lord.
And she was sent to tell others.
What a tragedy it would be to become so fascinated by a woman's imagined scandal that we overlook her actual witness to the resurrection.
And what a tragedy it would be to do something similar in our own lives.
To become so consumed by what people once called us that we forget who Jesus Christ is calling us to become.
Maybe you have spent years trying to prove that you are not the person people remember.
Maybe your past includes sins you genuinely committed.
Maybe your shame is not based on a false accusation at all.
Perhaps you really did betray someone's trust.
Perhaps you abandoned responsibilities.
Perhaps you lived in rebellion against God.
Perhaps you have been hiding behind religious activity while knowing that your private life needs repentance.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend those things never happened.
It calls you to bring them into the light.
Because biblical grace is not the denial of sin.
It is God's undeserved favor toward sinners through Jesus Christ.
And repentance is not merely feeling ashamed.
It is turning from sin toward God.
First John 1:9 tells us that if we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive us and cleanse us from all unrighteousness.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
And 2 Corinthians 5:17 teaches that anyone in Christ is a new creation.
These promises do not depend upon an invented biography of Mary Magdalene.
They rest upon the finished work of Jesus.
So whether your reputation has been unfairly damaged or your own choices have left painful consequences, your deepest hope is not found in rewriting history.
It is found in the Savior who entered history, bore sin upon the cross, and rose from the dead.
And if you have been carrying a secret burden, perhaps this is the moment to stop hiding.
You do not need to publish every private wound.
You do not need to expose another person's sins.
You do not need to tell strangers details that belong in a safe conversation with a trusted pastor, counselor, or mature believer.
But you can come honestly before God.
You can confess what needs confessing.
You can seek forgiveness.
You can make restitution where appropriate.
You can begin walking in obedience.
And you can trust that the mercy of Jesus Christ is greater than the label that has followed you.
There is another lesson in Mary's story that the Church must not overlook.
We must be careful with the names and reputations of people made in the image of God.
Proverbs 18:13 warns against answering a matter before hearing it.
Exodus 20:16 forbids bearing false witness.
And James 3 reminds us how destructive the tongue can become.
If we would not want our own stories distorted, we should be slow to distort the stories of others.
If we love biblical truth, we must be willing to correct familiar errors.
And if we proclaim grace, our words about other people should reflect truth, justice, and mercy.
Mary Magdalene's story challenges us to do precisely that.
It also challenges how we view women in the ministry of Jesus.
Luke does not erase the women who supported Christ's earthly ministry.
John does not erase the woman who announced His resurrection.
Their faithful presence matters.
Their testimony matters.
Their service matters.
And their stories deserve to be read as Scripture presents them, rather than reduced to stereotypes inherited from later centuries.
This is not about making Mary Magdalene the center of Christianity.
It is about refusing to miss what the Gospel reveals through her.
Jesus Christ is the center.
He delivered her.
She followed Him.
He was crucified.
He rose again.
He called her by name.
And she testified that He was alive.
That is more than enough to make her story unforgettable.
And now the question turns toward us.
What will we do with the truth we have heard?
Will we continue repeating a claim simply because it is familiar?
Will we let religious tradition speak more loudly than the biblical text?
Will we keep defining people by labels rather than seeking to understand their actual stories?
Or will we become believers who love Scripture enough to examine it carefully and love people enough to speak about them truthfully?
Not a faith built upon sensational claims.
Not a faith sustained by guilt.
Not a faith that confuses human tradition with the authority of God's Word.
But a faith continually brought back to Jesus Christ, repentance, grace, forgiveness, redemption, and the transforming truth of Scripture.
That is why your participation matters.
Perhaps a friend has believed this misconception for decades.
Perhaps a young believer needs to learn the difference between Scripture and tradition.
Perhaps someone who has been crushed by an unfair reputation needs to hear that Jesus does not require an invented scandal to demonstrate His grace.
Or perhaps someone who really has wandered into sin needs to hear that forgiveness is available through repentance and faith in Christ.
Which heart will be challenged.
Which conversation will begin.
Or which reader will open the Bible again because you shared something worth examining.
Not because a social media page can replace a local church, faithful pastoral care, or personal study of Scripture.
But biblical encouragement can help point people toward those essential parts of Christian life.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, prayer, spiritual maturity, and their daily walk with Jesus Christ.
The library is part of a larger desire to make Christian learning accessible, especially to people who may not have the financial means to purchase every resource they need.
That work takes time, care, and practical support.
And this is where those who have been blessed by Gospel Warrior's ministry can participate in a deeper way.

It is a voluntary, recurring contribution that helps sustain and expand the work of producing biblical teaching, developing discipleship resources, maintaining outreach, and making Christian materials available to more readers.
It may be part of your planned Christian giving, but it is not a mandatory biblical tithe, a replacement for supporting your local church, or a condition for receiving God's blessing.
You can glorify Him through faithful obedience, worship, service, generosity, and love in countless ways.
But if you believe this ministry is faithfully serving Christ, supporting it can be one meaningful way to participate in that work.
Remember the women of Luke 8.
Their giving was not what saved them.
Their service did not purchase His love.
It was a practical expression of their participation in His mission.
Not pressure.
Not spiritual bargaining.
Not a promise that giving money will make God owe you something.
But an opportunity to help biblical truth reach more people.
Those products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, tools for study, or meaningful gifts for people you love.
It is the possibility that a person who has never understood the Gospel may encounter the truth of Jesus Christ.
That someone who feels spiritually exhausted may find encouragement to return to Scripture.
That someone trapped in shame may hear about repentance and forgiveness.
That a believer who has inherited an inaccurate teaching may finally open the Bible and discover what it actually says.
You have not.
You can still pray.
You can still share.
You can still encourage someone.
You can still help spread the Gospel by speaking faithfully about Jesus Christ.
The invitation to come to Christ is freely offered.
What part of Mary Magdalene's story has challenged you the most?
Was it discovering that the Bible never calls her a prostitute?
Was it realizing how easily religious traditions can become confused with Scripture?
Was it seeing the faithfulness of a woman who followed Jesus and witnessed His resurrection?
Or was it something much closer to home?
The realization that you have been living under a name, accusation, memory, or shame that has become larger than the truth of who you are?
And if you have a testimony of repentance, restoration, or God's faithfulness, share what is appropriate.
Your words may encourage someone who is silently struggling.
No one needs to disclose private details to prove that their faith is sincere.
But sometimes a simple, honest testimony can help another person realize that they do not have to remain in spiritual isolation.
And now, one final thought.
Mary Magdalene did not stand outside the empty tomb with a carefully prepared speech.
She stood there weeping.
She did not initially understand what had happened.
She did not even recognize Jesus when she first saw Him.
Then He spoke her name.
And the woman who came looking for a dead body left announcing a living Lord.
That is the Gospel's unforgettable turning point.
The resurrection of Jesus Christ.
Not an invented scandal.
Not an embellished past.
Not a sensational reputation.
The risen Savior.
The One who calls sinners to repentance.
The One who forgives through His sacrifice.
The One who defeated death.
The One who remains worthy of our worship, our obedience, our testimony, and our lives.
So the next time someone tells you that Mary Magdalene was a prostitute, you can answer with both conviction and grace.
The Gospels never say that.
They say she was delivered from seven demons.
They say she followed Jesus.
They place her among the women who supported His ministry.
They identify her among the witnesses of His crucifixion and burial.
And John tells us that she encountered the risen Christ and announced Him to the disciples.
That is the story Scripture gives us.
And it is powerful enough without adding anything to it.
Perhaps the greatest tragedy is not that generations misunderstood Mary's past.
Perhaps it is that, while searching for a scandal the Gospels never recorded, they sometimes overlooked the miracle the Gospels unmistakably proclaimed.
The woman people remembered for a sin Scripture never assigned to her was remembered by Jesus as someone He called by name—and sent to proclaim that He was alive.
